briefs.label: Morning Brief
briefs.title: Relief on Two Fronts: Michigan's Tax Fight Goes Bipartisan While Psychedelics and M&A Power National Momentum
briefs.top: In Michigan, both major governor candidates are now on record against the 24% wholesale tax and Muskegon just broke ground on a $4M cannabis hospitality concept, even as Q2 tax revenue data shows the market slowly stabilizing. Nationally, Compass Pathways' psilocybin program is racing toward what could be the first-ever FDA-approved classic psychedelic, while a fresh wave of M&A signals capital is finally moving again.

local.text: Fields Cannary, a $4M dispensary-and-restaurant concept in Muskegon, is targeting a fall opening as a fully integrated cannabis hospitality model combining retail, on-site consumption, dining and event licensing — a bet that a winery-style elevated experience can support higher price points even under the new tax regime.

GOP gubernatorial nominee John James pledged to repeal or sharply reduce the 24% wholesale tax, calling it a levy that "drives up prices, gives illegal operators a competitive edge, and has already fallen far short of revenue projections" — putting both major-party candidates on record against the tax heading into November.

Michigan's wholesale tax generated $37.38 million in Q2 2026, up from $34 million in Q1 — still a fraction of the $105 million quarterly projection, but the upward trend is giving repeal advocates in Lansing fresh ammunition.

While Higher Love closed five of its nine Upper Michigan stores citing the tax hike directly, fellow U.P. operator Rize has kept growing by negotiating cost-sharing arrangements with suppliers instead of absorbing the tax alone — a survival playbook other multi-store operators are now watching closely.

A Republican state representative introduced House Bill 6224 to repeal the 24% wholesale tax outright, as CRA data shows active retail licenses statewide slipped from 845 to 836 over the past year — giving the repeal push real numbers to point to.

national.text: Compass Pathways' COMP360 psilocybin program hit positive 26-week durability results in July, and the company's rolling NDA is now targeting final submission in Q4 2026 with a potential approval by late 2026 or early 2027 — putting it on track to become the first classic psychedelic ever approved by the FDA.

Cannabis M&A hit a new gear in August: Curaleaf floated a $4/share cross-border bid for Aurora Cannabis while Grown Rogue struck a deal to acquire PharmaCann's New York license and four Verilife dispensaries for roughly $4.5 million — proof that rescheduling momentum and an improving capital backdrop are unlocking deals again.

DEA has begun sending detailed questionnaires to Colorado's state-licensed medical cannabis businesses that applied for federal protections under the April Schedule III order — the first concrete sign the rescheduling framework is moving from paper to practice for operators.

The House is expected to take up Senate-passed legislation this week to delay the scheduled federal recriminalization of hemp THC products, buying lawmakers more time to craft regulation as an alternative to an outright ban.

DEA's formal hearing on rescheduling marijuana to Schedule III wrapped in mid-July after weeks of testimony at DEA headquarters, and the industry is now waiting on the administrator's ruling — the single biggest swing factor left for U.S. cannabis markets.
